description: Cummins Inc. offers various power solutions worldwide. The company operates through five segments: Engine, Distribution, Components, Power Systems, and Accelera. It offers diesel and natural gas-power
description_full: Cummins Inc. offers various power solutions worldwide. The company operates through five segments: Engine, Distribution, Components, Power Systems, and Accelera. It offers diesel and natural gas-powered engines; and drivetrain systems, including axles, drivelines, brakes, and suspension systems; and on- and off-highway, and other products. The company also provides aftertreatment technology and solutions comprising custom engineering systems and integrated controls, oxidation catalysts, particulate filters, and selective catalytic reduction systems, as well as engineered components, including dosers; turbochargers, fuel systems, and valvetrain technologies; electronic control modules, sensors, and supporting software; and automated manual transmissions, and automatic transmissions for internal combustion engines. In addition, it sells and offers support services power generation systems, high-horsepower engines, and heavy-duty and medium-duty engines; offers application engineering services, custom-designed assemblies, and in-shop and field-based repair services; and retail and wholesale aftermarket parts. Further, the company offers standby and prime power generators, controls, paralleling systems, and transfer switches; turnkey solutions for distributed generation and energy management applications using natural gas, diesel, battery energy storage systems, and newer alternative sustainable fuels; diesel and natural gas high-speed, high-horsepower engines; and A/C generator/alternator products. Additionally, it provides electrified power systems, including batteries, fuel cells, and electric powertrain technologies. It sells its products to original equipment manufacturers, distributors, dealers, and other customers. The company was formerly known as Cummins Engine Company and changed its name to Cummins Inc. in 2001. Cummins Inc. was founded in 1919 and is headquartered in Columbus, Indiana.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 67K people. Revenue per employee of $500K ranks in the above the sector median among Industrials peers, with revenue growing 7%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $35K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $1K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 17× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: Cummins Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $55.3B market cap on $33.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 20% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 25% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $2.4B in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.27× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 12× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 1.9%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 12% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.07x).
It accounts for 0.9% of sector revenue and 0.9% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 29% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 45% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 1.01, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $642.4M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 21% in the 2022 bear market and 76% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $400 (margin of safety -1%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 17%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $251 to $635 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 16.8 vs 22.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 41% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 19 covering analysts target $620 on average, 54% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 9.4% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.35).
It runs a 25% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.27x.
ROE of 23% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.7x net debt to EBITDA ($3.6B of cash against $7.2B of debt), with interest covered 12.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.2% over 3 years, 11.2% over 5 years and 5.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 19.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.03, a backlog worth 19% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 10%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 3.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (13 sales, net $5.1M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.9% (2.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 41 consecutive years, raising it 6.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 67,400 employees, each generates about $500K of revenue, 1.4x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 7.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $8.6M (17x revenue per employee).
